title: Designing individual systems with AI
author: Alert_Masterpiece_38
selftext:
Hi,

I've seen a lot of posts where people "one shot" the initial game concept and work from there, but is there any guides or advice for building games system-by-system? One-shot results were not qute up to what I imagined, but when I tried doing things step by step, I've achieved even worse results. I can't even get the battle system from the ground, the Ai just can't replicate things it did when "one-shotting", even though I gave pretty detailed instructions. Am I doing something wrong?

I'm using Godot and Qwen 3.8Max through Qwen Code.

comments.author: Dangerous_Three_8506
comments.body:
I create documents with milestones and pictures. Can Qwen Code read pictures?

I don't have a document my own to share at the moment because they are my intellectual property. I have an example I can link you to.

https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f

Dont listen to the ignorant. The main part of the document is this here, its at the very bottom.

The right way to use this is to share it with your LLM agent and work together to instantiate a version that fits your needs. The document's only job is to communicate the pattern. Your LLM can figure out the rest.

What I learned is to work on documents every day that the whole world could feed into their AI and receive similar or the same output. The outputs are great works. 

In game combat, resources, etc...

comments.author: Hot_Professional8287
comments.body:
Yeah,. system by system is much better than one-shotting, but I'm surprised when you say you got a worse result when going step by step. 

How is that even possible? When you're running step by step.. you won't move to the next step until you're satisfied with the current step.

replies.author: Alert_Masterpiece_38
replies.body: In my case, I got stuck on refining the battle system, because I thought that there's little point on going forward with other stuff while the core is lacking. Thank you for advice, I'll have to spend more time on learning the technical side of things.

replies.author: Hot_Professional8287
replies.body: yeah, of course. I think what a lot of people haven't managed to "vibe" yet is learning. It's a feedback loop - the AI gives you more knowledge to make more accurate technical prompts, and you build more systems until you're stuck again -> repeat. You just keep climbing that way until you're speaking fluent Adeptus Mechanicus.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: I totally agree with you but I’m finding sometimes with the really good models that I get better results when I prompt less technically. I swear sometimes if you are too detailed with the prompt it tries too hard.

replies.author: ByteFoundry
replies.body:
I actually made a series of little experiments one prompt only states the goal "build me a game that ..." and the second prompt states goal and how "build me a game that ... using these technical concepts ..."

The first prompt in every model I tested created a visually more interesting result. But a horrible codebase.

The second one created a nice extensible codebase but had the looks as if a programmer had drawn the graphics. Simply more boring and bland to look at.

Tested this up to Opus 5 and Fable 5.1.

Of course one shotting anything is utterly useless and futile in itself. But I thought the experiments were interesting. As if the training data contains the info that programmers make bad art and therefore the results must look like it.

comments.author: Niedzwiedz87
comments.body:
Take a step back and try to think if you wanted to be able to read your code. You need to have the ability to understand what's it doing, use abstractions so you can more easily extend your game and add new functionalities.
Think architecture. What will be the components in your game? Read about MVC and MVP patterns - Model-View-Controller and Model View Presenter. 
Start your project by giving a general description of your game, and asking AI to help you do it step by step. Build a roadmap and a to-do list and ask AI to put it in the project.
Stop regularly to ask for explanations, for the purpose of each system, and for code audit. 
So far it seems to work for me.

replies.author: Alert_Masterpiece_38
replies.body: Thank you, I'll try doing that.

comments.author: Radiant_Function601
comments.body: My guess is you’re dealing with architectural drift.  Try to scaffold first, set up your rule structure initially.

comments.author: Avisolei
comments.body:
\> Qwen 3.8Max w/ qwen code

well that's one of your first problems....if you're at all serious about doing this drop that garbage, and start using an actual serious model + harness like opus 5.5 or astra w/ codex/claude code ( [https://artificialanalysis.ai/#intelligence](https://artificialanalysis.ai/#intelligence) ). Just tell the A.I you want to design a game system, you want it to do x,y,z and the key here is to get the A.I to ask you questions about the system so all of the ideas get fully fleshed out. Just work back and forth and pretend it's a colleague or classmate that you're working on a project with.

replies.author: Alert_Masterpiece_38
replies.body: Unfortunately Claude and GPT models are unavailable in my region, and using them through VPN results in a ban sooner or later, so I make do with what's at hand. Maybe Qwen 4 will save us.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: The scaffolds recommend are good, but even better if paired with documenting your whole game first. AI is great at reading text so if you right all the rules, ideas features, you can use that give your prompts a guideline. Vibe coding let's change  your whole code base in a single prompt, so it can be better as it grows to laser focus on just one feature, or part of a feature at a time.

replies.author: Alert_Masterpiece_38
replies.body: Thank you, I'll try that. But in my particular case, the problem I ran into were with elements of one documented system not behaving as they should.

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body: If you have something documented, expected to work a certain way, does anything test that after you rebuild? But it sounds like you might want to manage context. Make sure what you want the software to do is in a document in your repository. (and if you are not in a Git repository, I'd star there, being able to rewind is another way to get out of a small drift you didn't intent)

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: These one shots almost never show gameplay. Except the Minecraft one where the gameplay is completely emulated. Coming up with unique and fun ideas takes a lot of time.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I had a quick look through the GD-Agentic-Skills and it was pretty light on design detail for the part I looked at. It had some small code examples and a very brief description of each subject but that was pretty much it.

Maybe get your agent to explain which parts of the skill it is using and go have a look for yourself what the examples are showing. You are taking control of the process so you’ll have to get your hands more dirty.

Also, check your local hosting setup. Qwen can be really sensitive to temperature and reasoning value. If you’re already working with a local model I’m sure you’re in the right communities to get some suggestions here.

comments.author: KnownPride
comments.body:
I always do system by system.  
You start by creating the game core foundation, the core loop, than build up from there.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
There are 3 rules I follow when doing things step by step.

1.) Use the right AI for the job. Like using an text based AI for code, and an image or 3D AI for art. Don't use just one AI.

2.) Use the project options in your text AI, to make it forget about any other subject you have asked about. If your AI remembers the rest of the project, it will keep trying to use that information and mess up single steps.

3.) Make Checkpoints, the longer your conversation with AI gets, the longer and more inaccurate the next response will be, you will even start noticing mistakes more. So the idea is to reach some kind of checkpoint in the mechanic or code, that you can start an new conversation with the last one resolved.
